title: Payment Gateway Switch Cost: Marketplace Migration Guide & Risks
description: Switching payment processors? Estimate the real migration cost for marketplaces: engineering hours, token portability, zero-downtime parallel runs, and exit fees.
text: Migration cost · Marketplace Payment Processor & Gateway Switch Cost: What Marketplaces Pay to Migrate A payment gateway switch is rarely just an API key change. For marketplaces, the real cost sits in integration work, token portability, reconciliation rebuilds, parallel running, and contract exit terms. Last checked: November 2026 ← Back to calculator Clear context This guide covers migrating between marketplace payment processors and gateways, not core banking payment-switch infrastructure. Use it to estimate the switch cost before you commit, then compare your ongoing costs against your current setup. What a payment gateway switch actually costs The visible cost of switching is usually the new provider's pricing. The larger cost is the migration itself: engineering time, finance operations, customer payment data, dual-vendor overhead, and whatever your current contract says about leaving. For a marketplace, these costs compound because you are not only moving your own checkout. You may be moving merchant onboarding flows, split payments, payout logic, refunds, chargebacks, recurring mandates, and reconciliation across multiple seller accounts. A useful way to frame the decision is: switch cost is a one-off migration burden; ongoing cost is the run-rate you pay every month. A provider that looks cheaper on processing can still be expensive to leave, or expensive to run in parallel. The goal is not to find the lowest headline rate. It is to compare the total cost of moving with the total cost of staying. The five switch-cost buckets Engineering hours and API/webhook integration Estimate the work required to rebuild or adapt checkout, authorization, capture, refunds, chargebacks, webhooks, retries, idempotency, and test automation. For marketplaces, add split payments, seller onboarding, payout schedules, and any custom ledger logic. The hidden trap is not the first successful test payment. It is the edge cases: partial refunds, delayed capture, duplicate webhooks, failed payouts, and reconciliation exceptions. A clean Stripe Checkout integration can take 2–4 engineering weeks. A marketplace integration with split payments and payout logic typically takes much longer. Token portability and recurring payment data Payment tokens are not always portable between providers. If your marketplace stores tokens for recurring charges, subscriptions, or seller payouts, confirm what can be exported, what must be re-tokenized, and what requires customer re-authorization. The key question is not "can we export a CSV?" It is "can we keep recurring payments running without asking customers to re-enter payment details?" If tokens cannot move, forced card re-entry can cost you 15–30% of affected buyers . That turns a technical migration into a customer re-acquisition project. Reconciliation rebuild and finance operations Every switch changes how settlements, fees, refunds, chargebacks, and payout reports are formatted. Finance teams often need new reconciliation rules, new mapping tables, and new exception handling. The hidden trap is month-end close. If the old and new providers report differently, your finance team may run two reconciliation processes during the transition. Include accounting and operations time, not just engineering time. Parallel running and zero-downtime cutover Most marketplaces should not switch overnight. Parallel running lets you route a small share of traffic to the new provider, compare authorization rates, fees, and settlement behavior, then increase volume gradually. Zero-downtime migration requires feature flags, traffic splitting, rollback plans, monitoring, and customer-support scripts. The cost here is dual-vendor overhead: two dashboards, two settlement cycles, two sets of alerts, and two sets of contract obligations for the overlap period. Parallel running commonly lasts 4–52 weeks , and you pay both providers' rates on routed volume throughout. Contract lock-in, minimum commitments, and exit fees Read the current contract before estimating migration cost. Look for minimum monthly fees, volume commitments, early termination fees, hardware or integration fees, and notice periods. The hidden trap is a contract that is cheap to sign but expensive to leave. If the exit cost is high, the effective cost of switching is higher than the new provider's quote suggests. How to estimate your switch cost before committing Use a simple formula first, then pressure-test each input: Estimated switch cost = engineering hours × loaded day rate + finance/ops hours × loaded day rate + parallel-running months × dual-vendor overhead + contract exit costs + reconciliation rework Do not treat the result as a precise quote. Treat it as a decision range. Real migration projects typically run 23–37% over initial estimates , so add a buffer before you present the number internally. The table below is a static self-check you can use even without JavaScript. Cost bucket What to assess Common hidden trap Engineering API, webhooks, refunds, chargebacks, split payments, payout logic, test coverage Edge cases and retry/idempotency behavior, not the happy path Token portability Exportable tokens, re-tokenization, recurring mandates, customer re-authorization Tokens that export but cannot be used without customer action Reconciliation Settlement reports, fee mapping, refund/chargeback matching, month-end close Running old and new reconciliation in parallel longer than planned Parallel running Traffic split, feature flags, rollback, monitoring, support scripts Dual dashboards and dual settlement cycles for multiple months Contract Minimum commitments, notice period, exit fees, volume commitments Cheap-to-sign, expensive-to-leave terms For a marketplace, add one more check: who owns the merchant relationship after the switch? If seller onboarding, KYC, payout ownership, or customer support responsibilities change, include those operational costs in the estimate. One-off migration cost comparison by switch scenario Not every gateway switch costs the same. The one-off cost depends less on which provider you choose and more on what you are moving : tokens, recurring mandates, split payments, payout logic, and contract exit terms. The table below compares common marketplace switch scenarios using reference ranges from published implementation-cost analyses. Size / scenario Typical internal engineering Timeline Full one-off project estimate Relative burden Main driver SMB , simple gateway swap $15K–$80K 2–4 weeks ~$18K–$80K+ Medium API/webhook rebuild, settlement mapping Mid-market , ~500 accounts, custom integration $30K–$80K dev 2–4 months ~$80K–$160K+ High Reconciliation, parallel run, token handling Marketplace , orchestrated / split payments $75K–$200K 3–6 months $100K+ Very high Seller onboarding, payout logic, ledger rebuild Enterprise , acquirer certification $300K–$1.5M+ 6–12+ months $1.4M+ Very high Certification, PCI, 6–12 month parallel run How to read this table: "Very high" does not mean "do not switch." It means the cost bucket needs explicit estimation and owner sign-off before you commit. A high token-portability cost may still be worth it if the ongoing savings are large enough. The comparison is meant to stop you from treating every switch as a simple API swap. Two cost multipliers to watch Forced token re-entry: adds 15–30% buyer attrition cost if stored payment methods cannot be migrated. Timeline overrun buffer: adds 23–37% to the initial budget estimate due to edge cases and reconciliation delays. Sources: Ranges synthesized from published gateway implementation-cost analyses and marketplace integration guidance. Figures are reference ranges, not quotes. What is not included: Platform processing fees, FX margins, payout fees, or platform fees. Those belong in the ongoing-cost comparison in the calculator. Why a range, not a number: Migration cost depends on token portability, reconciliation complexity, parallel-run duration, and contract exit terms. Use the range to size the budget; use the five cost buckets above to refine it. Pre-signing checklist vs. switch cost: how to use both The pre-signing checklist is about what to verify before you sign a new provider contract: exit terms, data portability, pricing traps, and migration cost. This page is about the cost of the switch itself: what it takes to move, run in parallel, and retire the old setup. Use them together. Run the checklist before you commit, then use the switch-cost estimate to decide whether the migration burden is worth the ongoing savings.
